title: PPML-Omics: A privacy-preserving federated machine learning method protects patients’ privacy in omic data
authors: Zhou, Juexiao; Chen, Siyuan; Wu, Yulian; Li, Haoyang; Zhang, Bin; Zhou, Longxi; Hu, Yan; Xiang, Zihang; Li, Zhongxiao; Chen, Ningning; Han, Wenkai; Xu, Chencheng; Wang, Di; Gao, Xin
summary: Combines federated learning, differential privacy and shuffling of client gradients and applies it to bulk RNA-seq classification, single-cell clustering and ST-Net-style prediction of spatial expression from breast histology; attack experiments show that membership inference on a centrally trained model recovers expression differences. On the ST-Net task it used privacy budgets of 0.01 and 0.1 and reports mean squared error of 0.911 and 0.909 against 0.908 for central training and 0.926 and 0.910 for federated learning with DP alone, so all values sit near 0.91 and no per-gene correlation is given.
note: Full text read is the bioRxiv preprint version (PDF from Unpaywall); the published Science Advances version was not read. Only federated-histology-to-expression paper found.

title: Federated learning for computational pathology on gigapixel whole slide images
authors: Lu, Ming Y.; Chen, Richard J.; Kong, Dehan; Lipkova, Jana; Singh, Rajendra; Williamson, Drew F.K.; Chen, Tiffany Y.; Mahmood, Faisal
summary: Federated attention-based multiple-instance learning on whole slide images with Gaussian noise added to the weights before averaging, tested on breast and renal cell carcinoma subtyping across institutions. Federated training beat single-institution training; test AUC stayed at 0.927 to 0.932 (breast, n=321) and 0.986 to 0.988 (renal, n=170) for noise scales up to 0.1 times the layer weight spread, and I did not find an epsilon reported for the experiments.
note: Full text read is the arXiv version 2009.10190 (same title). Slide-level classification, not expression.

title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
authors: Kairouz, Peter; McMahan, H. Brendan; Avent, Brendan; Bellet, Aurélien; Bennis, Mehdi; Bhagoji, Arjun Nitin; Bonawitz, Kallista; Charles, Zachary; Cormode, Graham; Cummings, Rachel; D'Oliveira, Rafael G. L.; Eichner, Hubert; Rouayheb, Salim El; Evans, David; Gardner, Josh; et al.
venue: Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 14(1-2):1-210 (arXiv:1912.04977)
summary: Survey monograph by a large group of authors on advances and open problems in federated learning, covering systems and privacy considerations. The abstract states that federated learning embodies data minimisation but does not by itself settle privacy; I read only the abstract here.
note: Authors read from the arXiv listing (59 authors); Crossref lists only two. PDF of arXiv version 1912.04977 saved but not read beyond abstract. Seed (Kairouz et al. 2021).

title: Do Gradient Inversion Attacks Make Federated Learning Unsafe?
authors: Hatamizadeh, Ali; Yin, Hongxu; Molchanov, Pavlo; Myronenko, Andriy; Li, Wenqi; Dogra, Prerna; Feng, Andrew; Flores, Mona G; Kautz, Jan; Xu, Daguang; Roth, Holger R.
summary: Shows that earlier gradient inversion attacks stop working when clients update batch-normalisation statistics over several batches, and supplies a new baseline attack for that setting, evaluated on chest X-ray and fundus federated tasks. It also tests clients that train with DP-SGD, where reconstruction quality falls as noise grows, and treats the result as an upper bound on practical attack success.
note: Full text read selectively from arXiv version 2202.06924. Attack is on images, not on summary statistics.

title: Re-identification from histopathology images.
authors: Ganz, Jonathan; Ammeling, Jonas; Jabari, Samir; Breininger, Katharina; Aubreville, Marc
summary: Trains patch-based and multiple-instance models to predict the source patient of a histopathology slide on two TCIA lung cancer datasets and an in-house meningioma set. F1 for patient identification was 50.2 percent and 52.3 percent on the lung sets and 62.3 percent on meningioma, higher when test slides came from the same resection, and the authors propose a risk-assessment scheme for releasing slides.
note: Full text read is the arXiv version 2403.12816. Published DOI 10.1016/j.media.2024.103335. The authors note that models may be recognising the tumour rather than the person.

title: Anonymization of whole slide images in histopathology for research and education.
authors: Bisson, Tom; Franz, Michael; Dogan O, Isil; Romberg, Daniel; Jansen, Christoph; Hufnagl, Peter; Zerbe, Norman
summary: Sets out a guideline and an open-source library for anonymising whole slide images in common proprietary scanner formats under GDPR and HIPAA constraints. It treats slide labels and file metadata as the places where identifying information sits.
note: Preprint arXiv:2211.06103 (abstract also read). Published in Digital Health 2023, DOI 10.1177/20552076231171475.

title: Resolving Individuals Contributing Trace Amounts of DNA to Highly Complex Mixtures Using High-Density SNP Genotyping Microarrays
authors: Homer, Nils; Szelinger, Szabolcs; Redman, Margot; Duggan, David; Tembe, Waibhav; Muehling, Jill; Pearson, John V.; Stephan, Dietrich A.; Nelson, Stanley F.; Craig, David W.
summary: Shows that high-density SNP array data can reveal whether a person's DNA is part of a complex mixture, with a theoretical framework and experiments. It is the original demonstration that aggregate genomic statistics can expose membership.
note: Earlier than the 2016 range; included under the T6 range from 2006 because later included papers (Sankararaman 2009, Venkatesaramani 2023) build on it.

title: Genomic privacy and limits of individual detection in a pool
authors: Sankararaman, Sriram; Obozinski, Guillaume; Jordan, Michael I; Halperin, Eran
summary: Analytical and empirical study of the statistical power of tests that detect one individual's presence in a study group from reported GWAS summary data. It gives quantitative limits on how many markers are needed relative to pool size.
note: Included from 2006 range; later included papers build on it.

title: Privacy Risks from Genomic Data-Sharing Beacons
authors: Shringarpure, Suyash S.; Bustamante, Carlos D.
venue: The American Journal of Human Genetics
summary: Shows that beacon servers, which answer only allele-presence queries, still allow an attacker to infer whether a person is in the dataset. The attack needs the person's genotype and a modest number of queries.
note: Earlier than 2016; cited by Venkatesaramani 2023 and Beacon attacks.

title: Identifying Personal Genomes by Surname Inference
authors: Gymrek, Melissa; McGuire, Amy L.; Golan, David; Halperin, Eran; Erlich, Yaniv
summary: Shows that surnames can be recovered from personal genomes by profiling Y-chromosome short tandem repeats against genealogy databases, then combined with other attributes to identify people in de-identified sequencing sets. It is an early demonstration of identity from data released without names.
note: Earlier than 2016.

title: Quantification of private information leakage from phenotype-genotype data: linking attacks.
authors: Harmanci, Arif; Gerstein, Mark
summary: Argues that molecular phenotype data such as gene expression, usually assumed free of identifying information, can still be linked statistically to genotypes. It quantifies the private information leaked by such linking.
note: Abstract view truncated in my record; read to the sentence on statistical linking.

title: Bayesian method to predict individual SNP genotypes from gene expression data.
authors: Schadt, Eric E; Woo, Sangsoon; Hao, Ke
summary: Builds a Bayesian method that predicts individual SNP genotypes from RNA expression using published cis eQTLs. It shows genotypes can be inferred from expression data alone, which is the basis for linking expression profiles to genomes.

title: Assessing transcriptomic reidentification risks using discriminative sequence models.
authors: Sadhuka, Shuvom; Fridman, Daniel; Berger, Bonnie; Cho, Hyunghoon
summary: Introduces a discriminative sequence model that jointly uses all known eQTLs in a region to link gene expression profiles to genotype profiles, and compares it with earlier linking models. It reports higher linking accuracy across attack scenarios in datasets up to 22,000 individuals, suggesting earlier work understated the risk.
note: bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/2023.04.13.536784 (record also seen).

title: Private information leakage from single-cell count matrices.
authors: Walker, Conor R; Li, Xiaoting; Chakravarthy, Manav; Lounsbery-Scaife, William; Choi, Yoolim A; Singh, Ritambhara; Gürsoy, Gamze
summary: Shows that single-cell expression count matrices, once pooled into pseudobulk per cell type, can be linked to genotypes with public eQTLs, exposing phenotype information such as disease status. A genotype-prediction method that does not need eQTLs is also given, and variants from one study expose people in another.

title: Enabling tradeoffs in privacy and utility in genomic data Beacons and summary statistics.
authors: Venkatesaramani, Rajagopal; Wan, Zhiyu; Malin, Bradley A; Vorobeychik, Yevgeniy
summary: Notes that shared summary statistics such as allele frequencies, and beacon queries, remain open to likelihood-ratio membership inference. It introduces scalable approaches to choose how much to release or perturb to trade privacy against utility.

title: Haplotype-based membership inference from summary genomic data.
authors: Bu, Diyue; Wang, Xiaofeng; Tang, Haixu
summary: Proposes inferring whether a haplotype is present in a genome database from summary statistics such as allele frequencies, without needing the target's genome. It extends summary-statistic membership attacks beyond independent SNPs.

title: Inference attacks against differentially private query results from genomic datasets including dependent tuples.
authors: Almadhoun, Nour; Ayday, Erman; Ulusoy, Özgür
summary: Studies inference attacks aimed at differentially private answers to queries on genomic datasets. The abstract frames the work as testing whether DP-protected genomic query results still leak membership; my view of it is truncated.

title: Beacon Reconstruction Attack: Reconstruction of genomes in genomic data-sharing beacons using summary statistics.
authors: Saleem, Kousar; Cicek, A Ercument; Sav, Sinem
summary: Describes a reconstruction attack on genomic data-sharing beacons that recovers genomes from beacon responses. It adds to evidence that restricted-query releases still leak.
note: bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/2024.12.10.627379 also seen in Europe PMC.

title: Detecting the Presence of an Individual in Phenotypic Summary Data.
authors: Liu, Yongtai; Wan, Zhiyu; Xia, Weiyi; Kantarcioglu, Murat; Vorobeychik, Yevgeniy; Clayton, Ellen Wright; Kho, Abel; Carrell, David; Malin, Bradley A
venue: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium
summary: Shows that presence attacks that work on genome-wide summary statistics also work on summary data of clinical phenotypes. It is relevant because phenotype-level aggregates, not only SNP frequencies, can reveal who is in a study.

title: Unconditional latent diffusion models memorize patient imaging data.
authors: Dar, Salman Ul Hassan; Seyfarth, Marvin; Ayx, Isabelle; Papavassiliu, Theano; Schoenberg, Stefan O; Siepmann, Robert Malte; Laqua, Fabian Christopher; Kahmann, Jannik; Frey, Norbert; Baeßler, Bettina; Foersch, Sebastian; Truhn, Daniel; Kather, Jakob Nikolas; Engelhardt, Sandy
summary: Shows that unconditional latent diffusion models trained on medical images can reproduce copies of training patients' images. It is a documented memorisation risk for generative models used as data surrogates.
note: Relevant to synthetic-data routes rather than to a federated head.

title: Accessibility of covariance information creates vulnerability in Federated Learning frameworks.
authors: Huth, Manuel; Arruda, Jonas; Gusinow, Roy; Contento, Lorenzo; Tacconelli, Evelina; Hasenauer, Jan
summary: Introduces an attack on federated learning that works when the sample covariance of the clients' data can be computed from what is shared. This bears directly on schemes that share covariance-type sums.
note: My abstract view is truncated after the first sentences; PDF not retrieved. Bioinformatics 2023.

title: A federated learning architecture for secure and private neuroimaging analysis.
authors: Stripelis, Dimitris; Gupta, Umang; Saleem, Hamza; Dhinagar, Nikhil; Ghai, Tanmay; Anastasiou, Chrysovalantis; Sánchez, Rafael; Steeg, Greg Ver; Ravi, Srivatsan; Naveed, Muhammad; Thompson, Paul M; Ambite, José Luis
summary: Describes a federated learning architecture for neuroimaging analysis that adds security and privacy mechanisms for multi-site data. It is an example of a running multi-site federation in imaging.

title: Deep Leakage from Gradients
authors: Zhu, Ligeng; Liu, Zhijian; Han, Song
summary: Shows that the private training set can be recovered from publicly shared gradients in a few optimisation steps, for vision and language tasks, and discusses defences. It is the standard reference for gradient inversion.
note: Published at NeurIPS 2019; the venue is taken from citing papers (proceedings page not opened), so venue is secondary.

title: iDLG: Improved Deep Leakage from Gradients
authors: Zhao, Bo; Mopuri, Konda Reddy; Bilen, Hakan
summary: Improves deep leakage from gradients by recovering labels analytically before reconstructing inputs. It strengthens the attack in the single-sample case.

title: Inverting Gradients -- How easy is it to break privacy in federated learning?
authors: Geiping, Jonas; Bauermeister, Hartmut; Dröge, Hannah; Moeller, Michael
summary: Shows that images can be reconstructed from gradients of trained networks in federated settings, challenging the assumption that gradient sharing is private. It also examines how network architecture and batch size affect reconstruction.
note: Published at NeurIPS 2020 (venue secondary).

title: See through Gradients: Image Batch Recovery via GradInversion
authors: Yin, Hongxu; Mallya, Arun; Vahdat, Arash; Alvarez, Jose M.; Kautz, Jan; Molchanov, Pavlo
summary: Recovers batches of images from gradients using batch-normalisation statistics as a prior. It shows that averaging over a batch does not make gradients safe.
note: CVPR 2021 per citing papers (secondary).

title: Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models
authors: Shokri, Reza; Stronati, Marco; Song, Congzheng; Shmatikov, Vitaly
summary: Defines and demonstrates membership inference against trained machine learning models with black-box access. It is the standard reference for model-level membership inference.
note: IEEE S&P 2017 per citing papers (secondary).

title: Deep Learning with Differential Privacy
authors: Abadi, Martín; Chu, Andy; Goodfellow, Ian; McMahan, H. Brendan; Mironov, Ilya; Talwar, Kunal; Zhang, Li
summary: Introduces DP-SGD, training deep networks with clipped, noised gradients and a moments accountant for privacy loss. It is the primary reference for differentially private deep learning.
note: ACM CCS 2016 per citing papers (secondary).

title: Differentially Private Federated Learning: A Client Level Perspective
authors: Geyer, Robin C.; Klein, Tassilo; Nabi, Moin
summary: Proposes client-level differential privacy for federated averaging, hiding whether any single client took part. It adds noise at the aggregator.

title: Learning Differentially Private Recurrent Language Models
authors: McMahan, H. Brendan; Ramage, Daniel; Talwar, Kunal; Zhang, Li
summary: Trains recurrent language models with user-level differential privacy using federated averaging and reports only a negligible loss in predictive accuracy. It indicates that DP cost falls with many users.
note: Text data only; included as a standard DP-FedAvg reference.

title: Revisiting differentially private linear regression: optimal and adaptive prediction & estimation in unbounded domain
authors: Wang, Yu-Xiang
summary: Revisits differentially private linear regression and shows how the error depends on feature, label and coefficient domains, with adaptive versions of sufficient-statistics perturbation and posterior sampling. Experiments on 36 datasets favour the adaptive sufficient-statistics method (AdaSSP).
note: Preprint; no published venue verified here.

title: Differentially Private Ordinary Least Squares
authors: Or Sheffet
summary: Studies differentially private ordinary least squares, giving t-values and confidence intervals under random projections and under the Analyze Gauss release of the Gram matrix. It covers ridge regression via projection.
note: ICML 2017, PMLR 70:3105-3114; also arXiv:1507.02482 (abstract read).

title: On the Theory and Practice of Privacy-Preserving Bayesian Data Analysis
authors: Foulds, James; Geumlek, Joseph; Welling, Max; Chaudhuri, Kamalika
summary: Treats privacy-preserving Bayesian inference, including noisy sufficient statistics for exponential-family models. It is background for noise-aware inference on perturbed statistics.

title: Differentially Private Learning Needs Better Features (or Much More Data)
authors: Tramèr, Florian; Boneh, Dan
summary: Shows that linear models on fixed handcrafted features beat end-to-end differentially private deep networks at moderate budgets on image benchmarks; for CIFAR-10 it exceeds the best reported private network accuracy while improving the provable guarantee about 130-fold. It concludes that private learning needs either far more private data or features learned on public data.
note: Full text read selectively. ICLR 2021 (OpenReview page seen in search). Bears on a DP linear head over a frozen encoder.

title: Unlocking High-Accuracy Differentially Private Image Classification through Scale
authors: De, Soham; Berrada, Leonard; Hayes, Jamie; Smith, Samuel L.; Balle, Borja
summary: Studies DP-SGD for image classification and reports that scale and tuning raise accuracy under privacy. My abstract view is truncated, so the numbers are not recorded.

title: Medical imaging deep learning with differential privacy
authors: Ziller, Alexander; Usynin, Dmitrii; Braren, Rickmer; Makowski, Marcus; Rueckert, Daniel; Kaissis, Georgios
summary: Presents the deepee framework for DP-SGD in PyTorch and evaluates it on paediatric pneumonia classification and liver segmentation. It reports acceptable classification and excellent segmentation under rigorous privacy guarantees.
note: Full text PDF saved; read at abstract level only.

title: Differentially private federated deep learning for multi-site medical image segmentation
authors: Ziller, Alexander; Usynin, Dmitrii; Remerscheid, Nicolas; Knolle, Moritz; Makowski, Marcus; Braren, Rickmer; Rueckert, Daniel; Kaissis, Georgios
summary: Applies differentially private federated learning to multi-site medical image segmentation, noting that federated learning alone is not fully private. My abstract view is truncated.

title: Defending against Reconstruction Attacks through Differentially Private Federated Learning for Classification of Heterogeneous Chest X-Ray Data
authors: Ziegler, Joceline; Pfitzner, Bjarne; Schulz, Heinrich; Saalbach, Axel; Arnrich, Bert
summary: Shows that chest X-rays can be reconstructed from federated updates with deep leakage from gradients, most easily late in training, and adds Renyi differential privacy to the federated process. DenseNet121 reached AUC 0.937 at epsilon 6, about 0.03 below the non-private baseline, while ResNet50 reached only 0.76.
note: Full text read selectively. Preprint; published version not checked.

title: Privacy-preserving Federated Brain Tumour Segmentation
authors: Li, Wenqi; Milletarì, Fausto; Xu, Daguang; Rieke, Nicola; Hancox, Jonny; Zhu, Wentao; Baust, Maximilian; Cheng, Yan; Ourselin, Sébastien; Cardoso, M. Jorge; Feng, Andrew
summary: Examines privacy-preserving federated learning for brain tumour segmentation across institutions with differential-privacy techniques. My abstract view is truncated.

title: Cluster Based Secure Multi-Party Computation in Federated Learning for Histopathology Images
authors: Hosseini, S. Maryam; Sikaroudi, Milad; Babaei, Morteza; Tizhoosh, H. R.
summary: Proposes cluster-based secure multi-party computation for federated learning on histopathology images, motivated by leakage from shared parameters and gradients. My abstract view is truncated.

title: Proportionally Fair Hospital Collaborations in Federated Learning of Histopathology Images.
authors: Hosseini, S Maryam; Sikaroudi, Milad; Babaie, Morteza; Tizhoosh, H R
summary: Addresses hospital collaboration in federated learning of histopathology images where centers face data-sharing restrictions, using proportionally fair selection of collaborators. It is a federated pathology study, not on expression.
note: Checked against seed: Hosseini et al., TMI 2023, see Discrepancies for pages.

title: Differentially Private Simple Linear Regression
authors: Alabi, Daniel; McMillan, Audra; Sarathy, Jayshree; Smith, Adam; Vadhan, Salil
summary: Studies differentially private simple linear regression and compares estimators for fine-grained analyses of small subsets. It concerns one covariate, not high-dimensional ridge.

title: The Cost of Privacy: Rates of Convergence for Parameter Estimation with Differential Privacy
authors: Cai, T. Tony; Wang, Yichen; Zhang, Linjun
summary: Derives minimax rates for the cost of (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy in mean estimation and Gaussian linear regression, in low and high dimensions. It gives the privacy term in estimation error as a function of dimension, sample size and epsilon.
note: Published in Annals of Statistics per citing papers (secondary).

title: Private Regression via Data-Dependent Sufficient Statistic Perturbation
authors: Ferrando, Cecilia; Sheldon, Daniel
summary: Proposes data-dependent sufficient-statistic perturbation for linear regression based on privately released marginals and finds it beats data-independent perturbation. It also ties synthetic data to sufficient-statistic release.

title: Differentially Private Linear Regression with Linked Data
authors: Lin, Shurong; Paquette, Elliot; Kolaczyk, Eric D.
summary: Gives noisy-gradient and sufficient-statistics-perturbation algorithms for linear regression after record linkage, with error bounds separating linkage error, estimation error and the cost of privacy.
note: Published in Harvard Data Science Review 2024 per the HDSR page seen in search.

title: Enhancing Differentially Private Linear Regression via Public Second-Moment
authors: Cao, Zilong; Zhang, Hai
summary: Uses public data to improve differentially private ordinary least squares by estimating the second moment publicly. It reduces the noise cost of sufficient-statistics perturbation when public covariate data exist.

title: Differentially Private Regression with Unbounded Covariates
authors: Milionis, Jason; Kalavasis, Alkis; Fotakis, Dimitris; Ioannidis, Stratis
summary: Gives efficient differentially private algorithms for least squares and related regression with unbounded covariates, removing prior bounds on the covariates.

title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
authors: Dwork, Cynthia; Roth, Aaron
venue: Foundations and Trends® in Theoretical Computer Science
summary: Monograph that defines differential privacy and presents the standard mechanisms and their composition. It is the primary reference for the definitions used elsewhere in the literature.
note: Abstract from Crossref.

title: The future of digital health with federated learning
authors: Rieke, Nicola; Hancox, Jonny; Li, Wenqi; Milletarì, Fausto; Roth, Holger R.; Albarqouni, Shadi; Bakas, Spyridon; Galtier, Mathieu N.; Landman, Bennett A.; Maier-Hein, Klaus; Ourselin, Sébastien; Sheller, Micah; Summers, Ronald M.; Trask, Andrew; Xu, Daguang; et al.
summary: Review of federated learning in digital health, covering technical and privacy considerations and open challenges for clinical use. The abstract frames data silos and privacy as the barrier federation addresses.

title: Federated learning in medicine: facilitating multi-institutional collaborations without sharing patient data
authors: Sheller, Micah J.; Edwards, Brandon; Reina, G. Anthony; Martin, Jason; Pati, Sarthak; Kotrotsou, Aikaterini; Milchenko, Mikhail; Xu, Weilin; Marcus, Daniel; Colen, Rivka R.; Bakas, Spyridon
summary: Evaluates federated learning for brain tumour segmentation among multiple institutions against centralised training. It was one of the first multi-institution medical-imaging federated demonstrations.

title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
authors: Pati, Sarthak; Baid, Ujjwal; Edwards, Brandon; Sheller, Micah; Wang, Shih-Han; Reina, G. Anthony; Foley, Patrick; Gruzdev, Alexey; Karkada, Deepthi; Davatzikos, Christos; Sako, Chiharu; Ghodasara, Satyam; Bilello, Michel; Mohan, Suyash; Vollmuth, Philipp; et al.
summary: Federated training of a glioblastoma boundary-detection model across 71 sites, with no site data pooled. The data cannot be shared as a collection because of site restrictions, which makes it a working example of a federation under governance limits.
note: Site count from the nature.com page snippet; abstract view truncated.

title: Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
authors: Dayan, Ittai; Roth, Holger R.; Zhong, Aoxiao; Harouni, Ahmed; Gentili, Amilcare; Abidin, Anas Z.; Liu, Andrew; Costa, Anthony Beardsworth; Wood, Bradford J.; Tsai, Chien-Sung; Wang, Chih-Hung; Hsu, Chun-Nan; Lee, C. K.; Ruan, Peiying; Xu, Daguang; et al.
summary: Trains the EXAM model for COVID-19 outcome prediction on data from 20 institutes worldwide using federated learning, without sharing patient data.

title: Swarm Learning for decentralized and confidential clinical machine learning
authors: Warnat-Herresthal, Stefanie; Schultze, Hartmut; Shastry, Krishnaprasad Lingadahalli; Manamohan, Sathyanarayanan; Mukherjee, Saikat; Garg, Vishesh; Sarveswara, Ravi; Händler, Kristian; Pickkers, Peter; Aziz, N. Ahmad; Ktena, Sofia; Tran, Florian; Bitzer, Michael; Ossowski, Stephan; Casadei, Nicolas; et al.
summary: Introduces swarm learning, a decentralised scheme that avoids a central server, and applies it to blood transcriptomes and other clinical data. It is a documented multi-site approach for transcriptomic data.

title: Swarm learning for decentralized artificial intelligence in cancer histopathology
authors: Saldanha, Oliver Lester; Quirke, Philip; West, Nicholas P.; James, Jacqueline A.; Loughrey, Maurice B.; Grabsch, Heike I.; Salto-Tellez, Manuel; Alwers, Elizabeth; Cifci, Didem; Ghaffari Laleh, Narmin; Seibel, Tobias; Gray, Richard; Hutchins, Gordon G. A.; Brenner, Hermann; van Treeck, Marko; et al.
summary: Applies swarm learning to predict molecular alterations from routine histopathology slides across partners that keep data local. It reports the practical, ethical and legal obstacles that motivated decentralisation.

title: Towards fair decentralized benchmarking of healthcare AI algorithms with the Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge
authors: Zenk, Maximilian; Baid, Ujjwal; Pati, Sarthak; Linardos, Akis; Edwards, Brandon; Sheller, Micah; Foley, Patrick; Aristizabal, Alejandro; Zimmerer, David; Gruzdev, Alexey; Martin, Jason; Shinohara, Russell T.; Reinke, Annika; Isensee, Fabian; Parampottupadam, Santhosh; et al.
summary: Describes the FeTS challenge, with federated evaluation of segmentation algorithms across 32 institutions. Average generalisation was good while worst cases revealed site-specific failures.

title: Federated benchmarking of medical artificial intelligence with MedPerf
authors: Karargyris, Alexandros; Umeton, Renato; Sheller, Micah J.; Aristizabal, Alejandro; George, Johnu; Wuest, Anna; Pati, Sarthak; Kassem, Hasan; Zenk, Maximilian; Baid, Ujjwal; Narayana Moorthy, Prakash; Chowdhury, Alexander; Guo, Junyi; Nalawade, Sahil; Rosenthal, Jacob; et al.
summary: Introduces MedPerf for federated benchmarking of medical AI where models travel to the data. It shows evaluation at the data's home site as an operating model.
note: Abstract view truncated.

title: Federated learning and differential privacy for medical image analysis
authors: Adnan, Mohammed; Kalra, Shivam; Cresswell, Jesse C.; Taylor, Graham W.; Tizhoosh, Hamid R.
summary: Combines federated learning and differential privacy for medical image analysis including histopathology. My abstract view is truncated, so accuracy figures are not recorded.
note: Seed in oversight list (Adnan et al.).

title: End-to-end privacy preserving deep learning on multi-institutional medical imaging
authors: Kaissis, Georgios; Ziller, Alexander; Passerat-Palmbach, Jonathan; Ryffel, Théo; Usynin, Dmitrii; Trask, Andrew; Lima, Ionésio; Mancuso, Jason; Jungmann, Friederike; Steinborn, Marc-Matthias; Saleh, Andreas; Makowski, Marcus; Rueckert, Daniel; Braren, Rickmer
summary: Presents PriMIA, an open-source framework for differentially private, securely aggregated federated learning and encrypted inference on medical images, tested on paediatric chest X-rays. The abstract reports performance on par with locally, non-securely trained models.
note: Abstract read from the nature.com page.

title: Secure, privacy-preserving and federated machine learning in medical imaging
authors: Kaissis, Georgios A.; Makowski, Marcus R.; Rückert, Daniel; Braren, Rickmer F.
summary: Perspective on secure, privacy-preserving and federated machine learning in medical imaging, covering data-sharing limits from legal and ethical requirements.
note: Abstract view truncated.

title: DataSHIELD: taking the analysis to the data, not the data to the analysis
authors: Gaye, Amadou; Marcon, Yannick; Isaeva, Julia; LaFlamme, Philippe; Turner, Andrew; Jones, Elinor M; Minion, Joel; Boyd, Andrew W; Newby, Christopher J; Nuotio, Marja-Liisa; Wilson, Rebecca; Butters, Oliver; Murtagh, Barnaby; Demir, Ipek; Doiron, Dany; et al.
summary: Describes DataSHIELD, in which analysis code runs at each study's own server and only non-disclosive results return, to avoid pooling individual data. It is an established example of analysis at the data's home site.

title: The impact of site-specific digital histology signatures on deep learning model accuracy and bias
authors: Howard, Frederick M.; Dolezal, James; Kochanny, Sara; Schulte, Jefree; Chen, Heather; Heij, Lara; Huo, Dezheng; Nanda, Rita; Olopade, Olufunmilayo I.; Kather, Jakob N.; Cipriani, Nicole; Grossman, Robert L.; Pearson, Alexander T.
summary: Shows that deep learning features predicted from TCGA histology vary strongly by submitting site, because slides carry site-specific signatures. This bears on what identifies the source center in H&E.

title: International federation of genomic medicine databases using GA4GH standards.
authors: Thorogood, Adrian; Rehm, Heidi L; Goodhand, Peter; Page, Angela J H; Joly, Yann; Baudis, Michael; Rambla, Jordi; Navarro, Arcadi; Nyronen, Tommi H; Linden, Mikael; Dove, Edward S; Fiume, Marc; Brudno, Michael; Cline, Melissa S; Bimey, Ewan
summary: Commentary on federating genomic and health databases under GA4GH standards, where analyses run at each site and local results are aggregated. It says federation is justified only where data cannot be pooled for legal or technical reasons.
